feedback: If a learner knows which number is bigger but writes the sign backwards (for example says '7 is bigger' aloud but writes 4 > 7), this is an orientation slip, not a magnitude error: have them read the written statement aloud, notice it says the wrong thing, and turn the sign so its open end faces the larger numeral.
Confirm a correct placement by pointing to the number-line gap: the sign opens toward the numeral that sits further right.
Avoid relying on a 'hungry alligator eats the bigger number' story alone — use it, if at all, only alongside the number-line meaning, because the mnemonic without meaning leads to backward signs.
activities.intendedInsight: The comparison sign is not a picture to memorise: when the amounts differ, the open end of > or < always faces the larger amount — the numeral further along the number line — and when they are the same, = is used. Reading the completed statement aloud is how you check it is correct.
learnerActions: Keep the two numerals (with their towers/quantities visible) on the number line.
Choose and place the correct sign between them: >, <, or =.
Check the sign by its open end — the wide, open end should face the larger numeral/tower; the point faces the smaller.
Read the finished statement aloud exactly as written, for example '4 < 7' as 'four is less than seven'.
If what you read aloud does not match which number is actually bigger, flip the sign and read it again.
Try equal pairs so you also place the = sign.
activities.title: Place the >, < or = sign: > and < open toward the larger amount, = shows the amounts are the same

feedback: Correct responses for the prompts above are 4 < 7, 9 > 6, 3 < 8, each read correctly, and 2 identified as smaller than 5.
If a learner must still draw dots or count fingers for each numeral before deciding, the magnitude link is still forming — return to the number line rather than marking it wrong.
If a learner reverses specifically on 'which is smaller / less', rehearse both directions together on the number line until both phrasings feel equally natural.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the numeral-to-amount link is secure you can compare and order written numerals directly, without first building sets, and justify it by where each sits on the number line.
learnerActions: Given single-digit numeral pairs with no objects present — for example 4 __ 7, 9 __ 6, 3 __ 8 — decide for each which is greater or less and place the correct sign.
Read each completed comparison aloud ('four is less than seven', 'nine is greater than six', 'three is less than eight').
Answer 'which of 5 and 2 is smaller?' working directly from the numerals.
Put a short set of single-digit numerals in order from least to greatest.
Say how you know, using number-line position ('8 is further along when you count than 3').
activities.title: Compare and order from the numerals alone

feedback: Prompt for justification, not just an answer: 'how do you know 7 is more than 4?'
If the learner forgets equality is possible, offer an equal pair and ask whether one must always be bigger.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the comparison into words, including the possibility of equality, strengthens the link between the spoken comparison language and the written symbols.
learnerActions: Given two numerals or two small collections, say which represents more and explain your reasoning.
Use the words 'greater than', 'less than', and 'equal to' in your explanation.
Respond to follow-up questions such as 'which is further along when you count?' and 'could they ever be the same?'
activities.title: Talk it through: who has more, and how do you know?
